context_notes:
Surface find on private land. Research suggestions only, not an identification. Ranked: (1) orbicular chalcedony or 'eye' chert, Moderate: the rings are smooth, concentric chalcedony bands around white quartz cores, a common pattern where silica gel crystallized in layers around nuclei inside a nodule. (2) Silicified oncoids in chert, Low-Moderate: algal-coated grains replaced by silica also make concentric rings, but they usually show irregular wavy laminae and a fossil or grain nucleus. (3) Silicified colonial coral, Low: coral corallites show radiating septa (spoke-like partitions) and a honeycomb arrangement; none were seen in the daylight close-up. Natural, not worked: the edges are broken and water-worn with no striking platform, bulb or patterned retouch.

Central Texas context (general, not tied to this find spot): Elgin and Bastrop County sit on Cretaceous to Paleogene coastal-plain units, but the area's creek and terrace gravels carry chert and chalcedony washed in from Edwards Plateau limestones (Lower Cretaceous Edwards and Glen Rose groups) and from older gravels. Edwards-type cherts often hold silicified fossils, coated grains and banded chalcedony, so any of the three ideas is plausible for a gravel cobble. Which formation it came from cannot be told from photos.

How to tell chert/chalcedony from coral: (a) Use a 10x loupe on a ring. Radiating septa and a honeycomb of corallites point to coral; smooth concentric bands point to chalcedony. (b) Acid test: a drop of dilute HCl or vinegar should NOT fizz on silica. Fizzing means calcite, as in unsilicified coral or limestone. (c) Hardness: silica is about 7 and scratches glass; calcite (3) is scratched by a steel knife.

Research-only suggestions, not an identification, authentication or valuation.

Ranked: (1) chert cobble with an iron-oxide weathering rind, Moderate: the waxy-looking, pitted, orange-red cortex and rounded shape fit a stream cobble of chert whose surface has weathered and taken up iron stain. (2) Quartzite cobble, Low-Moderate: quartzite cobbles are common in the same gravels and can look similar on the outside; a fresh break would tell them apart (chert breaks with a smooth, conchoidal, waxy surface; quartzite is sugary and grainy with sparkle). A test flake scar or a battered end would be the sign to look for; none is visible in these photos.

context_notes:
Personal collection piece (brought from Nevada); not an Elgin surface find. Research suggestions only, not an identification. Ranked: (1) silicified petrified wood, Moderate (the evidence is strong, but confidence is capped at Moderate from photos): longitudinal fibrous grain, transverse checking (shrinkage cracks) and curved growth bands on the end grain are classic wood structures preserved in silica. (2) Fibrous or banded chalcedony, Low: chalcedony can be banded and fibrous, but it does not show cross-grain checking or growth-ring geometry. (3) Worked artifact, Very low: the edges are natural conchoidal breaks with no platform, bulb or patterned retouch.

Context (general): this piece is from Mark's personal collection, brought from Nevada (exact locality unknown). It is not a surface find from the Elgin property. Nevada has abundant Miocene petrified wood, roughly 10-20 million years old. It is preserved in Tertiary volcanic ash beds, where silica from the volcanic ash replaced the wood. Examples include Virgin Valley in Humboldt County, famous for opalized wood, and petrified wood in Esmeralda, Mineral and Nye counties. Opalized vs agatized: opalized wood (opal, hardness about 5.5-6) tends to be lighter for its size and may craze or crack as it dries out. Agatized wood (chalcedony, hardness about 7) scratches glass easily and is more stable. A careful glass scratch test on an inconspicuous spot can help. Palm vs hardwood: on a wet or polished end grain, palm shows scattered rod-like fibres (dots), while hardwood shows growth rings crossed by fine rays.

Research-only suggestions, not an identification, authentication or valuation.
